title: context-bumpy-warmup-runlog-mathias
body:
Goal:
- Quick scratch log for a small controlled experiment exploring a 'bumpy' warmup pattern: alternating short high-QPS bursts with low-QPS gaps to see how KV cache priming and GPU kernel steady-state interact. Trying to capture transient p95/p99 spikes and whether small prefill strategies reduce tail without hurting steady throughput.

Hypothesis:
- Short priming bursts (2–4 requests) spaced across 200–400ms can keep KV cache usefulness while avoiding sustained slot occupation. This might reduce p99 during later large bursts vs a cold start baseline.

Setup:
- Date: 2025-10-07 run, repeated 10x at different seeds.
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB (dedicated mini pool) with isolated nvlink off.
- Runtime: redwood-serving v1.9.3 (dev kernel picks on), batching on with max batch = 32, dynamic batch timeout = 6ms.
- Model: open-codec/gpt-small-8k-quant (int8-ish profile), seq len typical 512, avg tokens per request ~80.
- KV cache: enabled, prefix caching active, TTL not used for test.
- Test harness: local runner (bench/slot-scheduler) with poisson master and spike injector. Command snippet: 
  ./bench-run --pattern bumpy --burst-size 40 --burst-interval 1200ms --prime-bursts 30 --seed $SEED --out ./artifacts/run-$SEED.log

Patterns tested:
1) Cold baseline: start from clean process (no priming), steady arrival at 40 QPS for 5m.
2) Bumpy-primed: schedule repeating micro-prime bursts: every 14s run 4 bursts spaced 300ms apart of 8 requests each, then let main burst at t=60s of 40 QPS for 30s.
3) Aggressive-prime: same as (2) but 16-request micro-bursts.
4) Passive keepalive: single periodic ping every 30s (control).

Observations (raw):
- Cold baseline (avg over 5 runs): steady throughput achieved ~40 QPS after 12s warmup; p50 ~18ms, p95 ~142ms, p99 ~405ms. Noticeable p99 spikes correlated with first GPU kernel compilation warmups at t=3–6s.
- Bumpy-primed (5 runs): initial micro-bursts prevented the large compile spike in 4/5 runs; p50 ~20ms, p95 ~95ms, p99 ~168ms. CPU-side scheduling jitter visible around micro-bursts (small ~10–15ms bumps) but major tail reduced.
- Aggressive-prime (3 runs): slightly better p99 (~150ms) but steady-state p50 rose to ~23ms and observed occasional throughput wobble (3% drop) during priming periods.
- Passive keepalive: reduced kernel compile issues but did not reduce p99 as effectively as patterned micro-prime. p95 ~120ms, p99 ~260ms.

Sample trace excerpts (annotated):
- run-7.log (bumpy-primed):
  t=0.2s: micro-burst-1 start (8q) -> avg lat 28ms
  t=0.5s: micro-burst-2 (8q) -> avg lat 32ms
  t=1.1s: main burst steady -> p95 88ms
  t=13.0s: large burst -> p99 172ms (but no 4xx or CUDA OOM)

Throughput / latency table (median across runs):
- Cold baseline: steady-qps=40; p50=18ms; p95=142ms; p99=405ms; kv-hit ~0.02
- Bumpy-primed: steady-qps=39.5; p50=20ms; p95=95ms; p99=168ms; kv-hit ~0.21
- Aggressive-prime: steady-qps=38.8; p50=23ms; p95=88ms; p99=150ms; kv-hit ~0.29
- Passive-keepalive: steady-qps=39.9; p50=19ms; p95=120ms; p99=260ms; kv-hit ~0.06

Quick ascii sparklines (p99 over time, relative):
- Cold: ▁▂▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇
- Bumpy: ▁▁▂▂▃▃▃▂▂▁▁
- Aggressive: ▁▁▁▂▂▂▃▂▂▁

Notes / interpretations:
- Micro-prime bursts visibly raise early kv-hit-rate which correlates to reduced p99 for the later main burst. The effect scales with micro-burst size, but returns diminish and can hurt p50/throughput when micro-bursts are too large (slot contention + batching delays).
- Kernel compilation events (first use of specialized attention kernels) are the largest contributor to the worst early p99s; patterned priming helps by nudging the runtime into warm kernels before the big burst.
- The pattern is robust to different seeds but sensitive to micro-burst spacing: >600ms spacing loses effectiveness (cache eviction/slot recycling).

Open questions / next runs:
- Try hybrid: small micro-bursts at different shard times so not all replicas prime at same time (stagger by 100–400ms). Does this reduce contention further?
- Measure memory pressure / fragmentation during aggressive-prime to explain throughput wobble. Add nvprof traces.
- Re-run on 2x smaller GPUs (80GB -> 40GB) to see if prefill helps more/less.
- Try with quantized model variant w/o attention kernels compilation stage to isolate effect.

Quick TODOs:
- [ ] Add nvprof collection to bench-run (ticket JIRA-RT-4823).
- [ ] Create a small canary config for Dedicated pool to test staggered priming (PR referenced above).
- [ ] Share summary in #serving-runtime with plots and run artifacts (attach run-*.log + simple CSV).

Files produced:/artifacts/run-*.log (linked in GH PR), bench csv: artifacts/summary-bumpy.csv

Conclusions (working):
- Patterned micro-priming is a low-cost sensor/actuator strategy to reduce early p99 spikes for bursty workloads. For production: prefer many small micro-bursts staggered across replicas rather than a single large prefill. Tune to avoid steady-state throughput degradation.

Notes to self:
- Keep this in users/ until we have a tidy summary for eng-serving-runtime doc. Chat with Aisha about integrating into optimize suggestions (heuristic that recommends micro-prime when predicted burst probability > 30%).

End of scratchpad.
